query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the substrate to an optimal temperature range (250–350 °C) prior to APS deposition of the FeCoNiCrAl HEA will promote enhanced splat flattening and bonding, enabling the buildup of a thicker, uniform bond coat while maintaining minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat deposited using 15–45 μm feedstock via standard APS, which in the baseline condition yields insufficient coating thickness with acceptable oxidation levels.
generation.intervention: Preheat the substrate to an optimized temperature (250–350 °C) immediately before and during APS deposition, while keeping all other spray parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Atmospheric plasma spray (APS) deposition performed in either standard ambient or a controlled atmosphere below the oxidation threshold; the substrate is maintained continuously at 250–350 °C during the deposition so that the molten droplets spread more effectively upon impact.
generation.structural_mediator: The elevated substrate temperature reduces the thermal gradient experienced upon droplet impact, enhancing splat flattening and intersplat cohesion, thereby facilitating effective layer accumulation.
generation.mechanism: Preheating reduces the rapid solidification of the molten droplets, thereby allowing increased lateral flow and improved fusion with the preceding layers. This results in a thicker, denser deposit while still keeping oxidation minimal by operating within a controlled thermal window.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline using 15–45 μm feedstock without substrate preheating, the deposited coating should reach or exceed the required thickness with improved interlamellar fusion and reduced porosity, while preserving its chemical integrity and minimal oxidation levels.
generation.baseline: Standard APS deposition using 15–45 μm feedstock on a room-temperature (or unheated) substrate, which leads to insufficient coating thickness due to rapid droplet solidification and limited splat spread.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be effective as long as the substrate temperature is maintained within 250–350 °C, as temperatures above this range may trigger increased oxidation or other thermal degradation phenomena, while lower temperatures may not sufficiently improve droplet coalescence.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal substrate temperature within the 250–350 °C range, its interaction with other spray parameters (e.g., particle velocity, plasma temperature), and long-term adhesion and oxidation behavior under thermal barrier coating service conditions need further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled study by APS depositing FeCoNiCrAl HEA coatings on substrates at various preheat temperatures (room temperature, 250°C, 300°C, 350°C) while keeping all other spray parameters constant. After deposition, measure coating thickness, intersplat fusion, porosity, and surface oxidation levels.
measurements: Coating thickness via field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM)
Splat morphology and intersplat cohesion (via cross-sectional SEM analyses)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If preheating does not significantly increase the coating thickness relative to the baseline (e.g., lacking a statistically significant improvement) or if it leads to appreciable increases in oxidation or other degradation of coating integrity, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

Prior to spraying, the feedstock powder was dried in an oven at 200 °C for 3 h to remove the moisture and improve its flowability. First, 316 stainless steel cylindrical specimens with dimensions of Φ 25 × 7 mm were used as substrates. Before spraying, the substrates were cleaned with an ultrasonic cleaner in acetone for 10 min, and then dried with a dryer. To improve the bonding strength of the coating, sand blasting one side of the substrate was carried out to obtain a certain cleanliness and roughness. Generally, during atmospheric plasma spraying, heating of the plasma jet on the flying particles is stochastic. When the feedstock powder with a wide particle size range is injected into the plasma jet, different kinetic and thermal energy is obtained by the particles, which can cause different states. Fully molten particles with enough velocity will form the well-flattened splats, while unmelted or semi-molten particles will rebound or form the unmelted and semi-molten particles in the coating. In Figure 10c, all of the flattened splats and unmelted particles were mechanically bonded with each other, and a typical lamellar structure was formed. Comparing with the cross-section of the powder milled for 10 h (Figure 4b), the lamellar structure inside a single particle disappeared, and a splat with a uniform structure was formed, which indicates that elemental rearrangement took place after plasma spraying. proposals.intervention: Switch the feedstock to a coarser particle size distribution (e.g. 30–90 μm instead of 15–45 μm)
proposals.conditions: Maintain standard atmospheric plasma spray (APS) parameters, with the only change being the feedstock particle size; spraying in ambient or controlled atmosphere to keep oxidation minimal.
proposals.structural_mediator: Larger molten droplets form thicker splats on impact, resulting in enhanced intersplat bonding and overall increased deposit build‐up.
proposals.mechanism: Coarser particles have a lower surface-to-volume ratio and, when fully molten, yield thicker individual splats that promote a more efficient accumulation of coating layers; reduced oxidation risk is maintained due to the inherent lower reactivity of the larger particles’ surfaces during flight.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The deposited bond coat will reach or exceed the required thickness compared to the baseline feedstock while preserving a dense, well-bonded microstructure with minimal oxidation features.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By increasing the particle size, each deposited droplet contributes a larger amount of material per impact, directly overcoming the thickness shortfall without introducing additional processing steps that might compromise coating integrity or provoke oxidation.

proposals.intervention: Introduce an in-flight inert gas shrouding system (e.g., Argon or Nitrogen) around the plasma spray plume
proposals.conditions: Operate the APS process under the modified configuration in which an inert gas envelope surrounds the molten particles during flight; standard feedstock and spray parameters are used, and the gas flow is tuned to minimize oxygen contamination at ambient temperature.
proposals.structural_mediator: The inert shroud minimizes oxidation on the surface of individual droplets and enhances the thermal profile of the particles during flight, leading to improved flattening and intersplat cohesion upon impact.
proposals.mechanism: By shielding the molten droplets from ambient oxygen, the particles are less likely to develop surface oxides that inhibit interlayer bonding. This maximizes deposition efficiency, as particles retain optimal heat and chemical integrity, resulting in aggregates that build to a thicker deposit.
proposals.predicted_outcome: A thicker and chemically sound bond coat is achieved relative to the baseline 15–45 μm feedstock, with preserved microstructural integrity and minimal as‐sprayed oxidation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: The inert gas shroud directly tackles the dual challenge of insufficient thickness and oxidation; it improves deposition efficiency without altering the material composition or requiring multi-step post treatments.

proposals.intervention: Integrate an in-situ low-energy laser glazing (re-melting) step immediately after plasma spray deposition
proposals.conditions: After the APS deposition, expose the as-sprayed coating to a controlled laser re-melting pass in an inert (e.g., Argon) chamber; laser parameters (energy density, spot size, scan speed) are optimized to re-melt surface splats without causing excessive oxidation.
proposals.structural_mediator: Laser glazing fuses adjacent splats and consolidates micro-voids, effectively ‘thickening’ the coating by improving the continuity and homogeneity of the deposit.
proposals.mechanism: The brief laser re-melting locally reflows the deposited material, allowing it to coalesce more completely. This leads to a thicker, more continuous layer as individual splats merge, while the inert atmosphere limits oxygen ingress.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The bond coat exhibits increased overall thickness and densification over the unglazed baseline while retaining a minimal oxide content and high adhesion, making it fit for service in thermal barrier coating systems.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By re-melting and fusing the as-sprayed material, this single post-deposition intervention overcomes the thickness limitation without introducing new oxidation issues; it directly addresses the microstructural inefficiencies that lead to thickness shortfall.

proposals.intervention: Preheat the substrate to an optimized elevated temperature (e.g., 250–350 °C) prior to deposition
proposals.conditions: Carry out APS deposition with the substrate maintained at this elevated temperature (below the oxidation threshold for the alloy) in the standard ambient or controlled atmosphere; all other spray parameters remain constant.
proposals.structural_mediator: Elevated substrate temperature enhances splat flattening and bonding due to a reduced thermal gradient, leading to better intersplat cohesion and layer accumulation.
proposals.mechanism: A pre-heated substrate reduces the rapid solidification rate of incoming droplets, promoting improved wetting and spread, which results in a thicker, more uniform coating. The controlled temperature also minimizes thermal stresses and potential oxidation due to a gentler thermal profile.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The deposited coating will build up to the desired thickness with improved interlamellar fusion and reduced porosity, while maintaining chemical and microstructural integrity with minimal oxidation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: Optimizing the substrate preheat is a single process adjustment that directly enhances deposition efficiency and thickness build-up without altering the feedstock or compromising oxidation resistance, directly addressing the coating shortfall.

decision.rationale: Among the proposed directions, preheating the substrate (Direction A) offers a single, straightforward process modification that directly improves the splat flattening and intersplat cohesion necessary for building up the desired coating thickness. By elevating the substrate temperature (while keeping it below the oxidation threshold), the rapid cooling and solidification of the molten droplets can be moderated. This enables increased lateral spread, better bonding between splats, and ultimately a thicker, more uniform deposit, all while preserving the minimal as‐sprayed oxidation. The mechanism is directly tied to controlling the thermal gradient at impact, and the literature on APS coating morphology (e.g., observations of splat formation and surface roughness described in the eligible records) supports the importance of substrate temperature on deposit structure and adhesion. Although other directions (laser glazing, feedstock coarsening, or inert gas shrouding) bring valuable ideas, preheating is a more controlled and less invasive adjustment, with fewer risks of introducing new defects or oxidation issues.
